newsitem.title: USA: Mercury reduces debt principal, makes payments.
newsitem.headline: Mercury reduces debt principal, makes payments.

text.p: Mercury Finance Co., the troubled auto finance company, said Tuesday it agreed to pay its creditors $70 million to reduce its outstanding debt and bring its interest payments current.

The Chicago-based company, which recently disclosed it had vastly overstated earnings for four consecutive years, said it also agreed, depending on its cash flow, to make additional periodic payments to reduce principal.
Creditors pledged not to take action against Mercury under their debt agreements prior to Oct. 1, at which time the forbearance agreement may be renewed, Mercury said.
The Chicago-based company has $933.6 million of debt outstanding.

Mercury said its creditors granted an extension to Sept. 30 of waivers, permitting it to continue to pledge assets as collateral on its credit facility with the Bank of America. No funds are currently outstanding under the facility.

Mercury specialises in the subprime auto finance market, making loans at high interest rates to car buyers who cannot borrow money elsewhere. The company has repeatedly delayed releasing its 1996 annual report, prompting speculation that the accounting irregularities that plunged the company into financial crisis in January were known at the highest levels of management.
Mercury gave no date for the release of its income statements. But the company released its 1996 balance sheet, reflecting year-end shareholders' equity of $168.9 million.
Mercury said the only significant difference from an April 23 estimate comes from a decision to book the loss from the Lyndon Insurance sale in 1997 rather than 1996.

The balance sheet was audited by independent public accountant Arthur Andersen LLP. In line with the company's disclosure on April 23, the auditor's opinion contains language questioning Mercury's ability to continue as a going concern.
Mercury said release of the income statement for the year has been delayed pending the resolution of timing issues related to recognition of revenues and expenses between 1995 and 1996.

The company said it has been engaged in informal discussions with the Securities and Exchange Commission and continues to work with Arthur Andersen LLP and KPMG Peat Marwick, its auditor for the years prior to 1996, to resolve allocation issues.
The company said it expects to issue results from the first quarter of 1997 in about one week.
Mercury's stock was off 12.5 cents at $2.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
